## Solution

We estimate the first positive zero of

$$f(x)=\int_0^\infty \cos(tx)\,e^{-t^4}\,dt.$$

### 1. Analytical setup

Since $e^{-t^4}$ is even,

$$f(x)=\frac12\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{itx}e^{-t^4}\,dt,$$

i.e. $2f(x)$ is the Fourier transform of the bump $e^{-t^4}$. The bump decays on the scale $t\sim 1$ (since $e^{-1^4}=0.37$, $e^{-1.5^4}\approx 0.006$), so its transform has its first zero at $x=\Theta(\pi)\approx 3.1$–$3.5$. A crude "hard cutoff" model $\int_0^T\cos(tx)\,dt=\sin(Tx)/x$ gives the first zero at $x=\pi/T$; with effective support $T\approx 0.92$ (where $e^{-T^4}\approx e^{-0.72}\approx 0.49$, the half-max point) this already yields $x\approx \pi/0.92\approx 3.41$, matching the hint. To pin it down we evaluate $f$ directly.

### 2. Scaling reduction

Substituting $u=tx$ ($dt=du/x$),

$$f(x)=\frac1x\int_0^\infty \cos(u)\,e^{-(u/x)^4}\,du \;=:\;\frac{I(x)}{x},\qquad I(x)=\int_0^\infty \cos(u)\,e^{-u^4/x^4}\,du.$$

For $x\in[3.4,3.5]$ the factor $e^{-u^4/x^4}$ suppresses the integrand beyond $u\approx 7$, so $I(x)$ is a finite, well-behaved integral that we evaluate by the trapezoidal rule with step $h=0.5$ on $[0,7]$.

### 3. Numerical quadrature

Computing $g(u)=\cos(u)\,e^{-(u/x)^4}$ at $u=0,0.5,\dots,7$:

- **$x=3.4$** ($x^4=133.6$): the sampled values give
 $$I(3.4)\approx \tfrac{0.5}{2}\big[g(0)+g(7)+2\sum_{k=1}^{13}g(0.5k)\big]\approx 0.0334,$$
 $$f(3.4)=I(3.4)/3.4\approx +0.0098.$$

- **$x=3.5$** ($x^4=150.1$): similarly
 $$I(3.5)\approx -0.0286,\qquad f(3.5)=I(3.5)/3.5\approx -0.0082.$$

- **$x=3.45$** ($x^4=141.7$):
 $$I(3.45)\approx 0.0021,\qquad f(3.45)\approx +0.0006.$$

The trapezoidal error here is $\lesssim 1.5\times10^{-3}$ in $f$ (the integrand has period $\approx 2\pi$, so $h=0.5$ gives $\sim 12$ points per period). Thus

$$f(3.4)=+0.0098\pm0.0015,\quad f(3.45)=+0.0006\pm0.0015,\quad f(3.5)=-0.0082\pm0.0015.$$

### 4. Bracketing the zero

$f$ changes sign between $x=3.4$ and $x=3.5$, with $f(3.45)$ essentially zero (within the quadrature error). Linear interpolation between the two robustly-signed endpoints gives

$$x_0 \;\approx\; 3.4 + \frac{0.0098}{0.0098+0.0082}\cdot 0.1 \;\approx\; 3.45.$$

Refining with the near-zero value at $3.45$ places the root at roughly $x_0\approx 3.45$–$3.46$.

### 5. Conclusion

The first positive zero of $f(x)=\int_0^\infty \cos(tx)e^{-t^4}\,dt$ lies at approximately

$$\boxed{x_0 \approx 3.45}$$

(in the interval $[3.4,\,3.5]$), consistent with the numerical suggestion of $\sim 3.4$. The estimate rests on (i) recognizing $f$ as half the Fourier transform of a width-$\sim1$ bump, which forces the first zero to $O(\pi)$, and (ii) a direct trapezoidal evaluation of the scaled integral $I(x)=\int_0^\infty \cos(u)e^{-(u/x)^4}\,du$ at $x=3.4,3.45,3.5$, which exhibits a clean sign change.

### PROOF COMPLETE

## Solution

We estimate the first positive zero of

$$f(x)=\int_0^\infty \cos(tx)\,e^{-t^4}\,dt.$$

### 1. Analytical setup

Since $e^{-t^4}$ is even,

$$f(x)=\frac12\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{itx}e^{-t^4}\,dt,$$

i.e. $2f(x)$ is the Fourier transform of the bump $e^{-t^4}$. The bump decays on the scale $t\sim 1$ (since $e^{-1^4}=0.37$, $e^{-1.5^4}\approx 0.006$), so its transform has its first zero at $x=\Theta(\pi)\approx 3.1$–$3.5$. A crude "hard cutoff" model $\int_0^T\cos(tx)\,dt=\sin(Tx)/x$ gives the first zero at $x=\pi/T$; with effective support $T\approx 0.92$ (where $e^{-T^4}\approx e^{-0.72}\approx 0.49$, the half-max point) this already yields $x\approx \pi/0.92\approx 3.41$, matching the hint. To pin it down we evaluate $f$ directly.

### 2. Scaling reduction

Substituting $u=tx$ ($dt=du/x$),

$$f(x)=\frac1x\int_0^\infty \cos(u)\,e^{-(u/x)^4}\,du \;=:\;\frac{I(x)}{x},\qquad I(x)=\int_0^\infty \cos(u)\,e^{-u^4/x^4}\,du.$$

For $x\in[3.4,3.5]$ the factor $e^{-u^4/x^4}$ suppresses the integrand beyond $u\approx 7$, so $I(x)$ is a finite, well-behaved integral that we evaluate by the trapezoidal rule with step $h=0.5$ on $[0,7]$.

### 3. Numerical quadrature

Computing $g(u)=\cos(u)\,e^{-(u/x)^4}$ at $u=0,0.5,\dots,7$:

- **$x=3.4$** ($x^4=133.6$): the sampled values give
 $$I(3.4)\approx \tfrac{0.5}{2}\big[g(0)+g(7)+2\sum_{k=1}^{13}g(0.5k)\big]\approx 0.0334,$$
 $$f(3.4)=I(3.4)/3.4\approx +0.0098.$$

- **$x=3.5$** ($x^4=150.1$): similarly
 $$I(3.5)\approx -0.0286,\qquad f(3.5)=I(3.5)/3.5\approx -0.0082.$$

- **$x=3.45$** ($x^4=141.7$):
 $$I(3.45)\approx 0.0021,\qquad f(3.45)\approx +0.0006.$$

The trapezoidal error here is $\lesssim 1.5\times10^{-3}$ in $f$ (the integrand has period $\approx 2\pi$, so $h=0.5$ gives $\sim 12$ points per period). Thus

$$f(3.4)=+0.0098\pm0.0015,\quad f(3.45)=+0.0006\pm0.0015,\quad f(3.5)=-0.0082\pm0.0015.$$

### 4. Bracketing the zero

$f$ changes sign between $x=3.4$ and $x=3.5$, with $f(3.45)$ essentially zero (within the quadrature error). Linear interpolation between the two robustly-signed endpoints gives

$$x_0 \;\approx\; 3.4 + \frac{0.0098}{0.0098+0.0082}\cdot 0.1 \;\approx\; 3.45.$$

Refining with the near-zero value at $3.45$ places the root at roughly $x_0\approx 3.45$–$3.46$.

### 5. Conclusion

The first positive zero of $f(x)=\int_0^\infty \cos(tx)e^{-t^4}\,dt$ lies at approximately

$$\boxed{x_0 \approx 3.45}$$

(in the interval $[3.4,\,3.5]$), consistent with the numerical suggestion of $\sim 3.4$. The estimate rests on (i) recognizing $f$ as half the Fourier transform of a width-$\sim1$ bump, which forces the first zero to $O(\pi)$, and (ii) a direct trapezoidal evaluation of the scaled integral $I(x)=\int_0^\infty \cos(u)e^{-(u/x)^4}\,du$ at $x=3.4,3.45,3.5$, which exhibits a clean sign change.
